title: Latches and flip-flops
kicker: ENEX 152 · Digital Logic · Sequential Logic Circuits
subtitle: Combinational logic has no memory. Feed an output back to an input and you get a circuit that remembers.

sections.title: Memory from feedback
sections.body: A combinational output depends only on the present inputs. A sequential circuit’s output also depends on its state — what happened before — stored in latches or flip-flops. The simplest memory is two cross-coupled NOR (or NAND) gates: each output feeds the other’s input, so the pair holds whichever state it was last pushed into.

choices.text: Its output depends on stored state, not only current inputs.

sections.title: The SR latch
sections.body: Inputs S (set) and R (reset): S = 1 forces Q = 1; R = 1 forces Q = 0; S = R = 0 holds the previous Q; S = R = 1 is forbidden (both outputs collapse, and releasing both at once is unpredictable). Toggle S and R below and watch Q remember.

worked.why: Start with Q = 0. Set S = 1, R = 0 → Q = 1. Return S to 0.
With S = R = 0 the latch holds Q = 1: memory.

questions.prompt: Which SR input combination is forbidden?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Both outputs are forced the same way.

figures.caption: Figure 3.2.1 — SR latch
figures.note: Pulse S to 1 then back to 0: Q stays 1.

sections.title: Gated latch and the D flip-flop
sections.body: A D latch is transparent while the enable is high — its output follows D. A D flip-flop is edge-triggered: it samples D only at the clock’s rising edge and holds it until the next. Edge triggering makes whole systems predictable: every flip-flop changes at the same instant.

choices.text: Only at the active clock edge.

figures.caption: Figure 3.3.1 — D flip-flop
figures.note: Change D between clock edges: Q only follows on a rising edge.

sections.title: JK and T flip-flops
sections.body:
J KNext Q
0 0Q (hold)
0 10 (reset)
1 01 (set)
1 1Q′ (toggle)

The JK fixes the forbidden state by making 1,1 toggle. Tie J and K together and you get a T flip-flop: T = 1 toggles every clock, which halves the frequency.

worked.why: A T flip-flop with T = 1 is clocked at 8 MHz.
Q toggles once per clock, so one full Q cycle takes two clocks.

questions.prompt: J = K = 1 makes a JK flip-flop…

problems.prompt: Three T flip-flops (T = 1) are cascaded, each clocked by the previous output, starting from a 24 MHz clock. Frequency at the last output?

sections.title: Setup and hold time
sections.body: D must be stable for a setup time before the clock edge and a hold time after it, or the flip-flop may go metastable (neither 0 nor 1 for a while). The clock period must cover clock-to-Q delay + logic delay + setup time.

worked.why: t_cq = 2 ns, logic = 8 ns, setup = 1 ns.
Minimum period = 11 ns, so f_max ≈ 91 MHz.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: It is a real failure mode.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: D changed too close to the edge.

sections.title: Characteristic tables and excitation
sections.body: The characteristic equation gives the next state: D: Q⁺ = D; T: Q⁺ = T⊕Q; JK: Q⁺ = JQ′ + K′Q. The excitation table runs the other way: given the wanted transition Q → Q⁺, what inputs are needed? For JK, 0→1 needs J = 1 (K = X); 1→0 needs K = 1 (J = X). Used when designing counters and state machines.

questions.prompt: A JK flip-flop must go 0 → 1. Which inputs work?
